report:
### Conclusion
Extensive epidemiological and clinical research confirms that increasing the number of childhood vaccines—or receiving multiple vaccines according to the recommended immunization schedule—does not increase the risk of autism spectrum disorder (ASD).

### Evidence Summary
- **Antigen Load ("Too Many Too Soon"):** A landmark study published in *The Journal of Pediatrics* directly investigated whether cumulative exposure to vaccine antigens during early childhood increases autism risk. Researchers measured total exposure to antibody-stimulating proteins and polysaccharides in children during their first two years of life and found no association with ASD risk.
- **Population-Based & Cohort Studies:** Large-scale national population studies (such as Danish cohort studies involving hundreds of thousands of children) have repeatedly evaluated both single vaccines (like MMR) and total vaccine schedules. These studies consistently demonstrate that vaccinated children have the same rate of autism as unvaccinated children.
- **Vaccine Components:** Comprehensive reviews by major medical institutions, including the Institute of Medicine (now the National Academy of Medicine) and the CDC, have evaluated specific components—such as thimerosal and aluminum adjuvants—and found no causal link to autism.

The global medical consensus is that recommended childhood vaccination schedules are safe and do not cause autism.

### Sources
- *The Journal of Pediatrics* (Study on Immunologic Stimulation and Autism Risk): https://www.jpeds.com/article/s0022-3476(13)00144-3/fulltext
- Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC Vaccine Studies Summary): https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/vaccinesafety/00_pdf/CDCStudiesonVaccinesandAutism.pdf
- PubMed Central (Review on MMR Vaccine and Autism): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6768751/
- Healthline (Report on Large Population Vaccine Safety Studies): https://www.healthline.com/health-news/research-finds-no-evidence-vaccines-cause-autism
